prompt: A program like lesson 1's `visitors.py` counts the different visitors of each book over five years of clicks, and dies with `MemoryError` on a machine that cannot be made larger. Which change lets the same machine finish with the right counts?
hint: Big Data and Distributed Processing, lesson 1.

choices.text: Split the input by day, count each day's different visitors, and add the daily counts
choices.why: A visitor who came on two days is counted on both. Only a split by the visitor puts each visitor in exactly one part, which is what lets the counts add up.

choices.text: Keep the visitors in a more compact structure than a set of strings
choices.why: A smaller structure moves the wall and does not remove it: five years of visitors still have to be held at once.

choices.text: Read the daily files one at a time, closing each before opening the next
choices.why: The files are not what fills memory. The sets keep growing across every file, and they are only counted at the end.

choices.text: Hash each visitor into one of sixteen files, count each file alone, and add the counts
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Each purchase once, because Spark undoes a lost task's writes before it reruns the task
choices.why: Spark knows nothing of a side effect. The rerun writes again, and the rows of the first attempt stay where they are.

choices.text: Some purchases missing, because a task lost with its executor is not run again
choices.why: The driver sends a lost task to another executor; lesson 2 watched it happen and got the right answer.

choices.text: Some purchases twice; `spark.task.maxFailures` set to 1, so that no task ever runs a second time
choices.why: Then one lost executor fails the whole job, and the rows the dead attempt wrote stay in the table anyway.

choices.text: Some purchases twice; inserting each keyed by its sale id with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A job writes a year of clicks with `partitionBy("day")` straight after `repartition(50)`, and leaves fifty files in every day's directory. Which change gives each day one file?
hint: Big Data and Distributed Processing, lesson 8.

choices.why: `repartition(50)` names its own count, so the setting changes nothing here; and more tasks holding every day would only mean more files.

choices.text: `spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile` set to a day's rows

choices.text: `repartition(365)`, so that there is one task for each day
choices.why: Without a column the rows are dealt out in turn, not by day, so each of the 365 tasks holds rows of every day.

choices.text: `repartition("day")` before the write
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A Structured Streaming query keeps a `checkpointLocation`, and lesson 9's loop calls `rank.checkpoint()`. What does the streaming checkpoint hold that the loop's does not?

choices.text: Which offsets each batch read, whether its output reached the sink, and the open windows

choices.text: Nothing different: both cut a lineage that has grown too long

choices.text: The same kind of data, kept on the driver's local disk

prompt: In PostgreSQL the analyst role was granted six columns of `sales.customers`, and `email` is not one of them. A nightly Spark job copies the whole table to Parquet in the lake, and an analyst runs `spark.read.parquet(path).select("email")`. What happens?

choices.text: The e-mails come back: the grant is checked by PostgreSQL, not by a file
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nulls: column pruning leaves out what a role was not granted
choices.why: Pruning drops the columns a query does not use, and this query uses `email`.

choices.text: Refused: the copy was made with the analyst's grants, so `email` never reached the lake
choices.why: The job copied the whole table as a role that may read all of it. What the analyst may see was never part of the copy.

prompt: Match each second run to what a reader sees after it.

pairs.right: One copy: the log already holds the pair, so nothing is written

prompt: Visitor `v0936542` asks to be forgotten. The team runs `DELETE FROM` on the Delta table of clicks, the commit succeeds, and they reply that the data is gone. What is still true?
hint: Big Data and Distributed Processing, lesson 11; Data Security, Governance and Privacy, lesson 7.

choices.text: `VERSION AS OF` an earlier version returns the rows, until `VACUUM` deletes the old files past their retention
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing: the delete rewrote every file that held the rows, so no copy of them is left
choices.why: The rewrite added new files and marked the old ones removed; they stay on disk, and time travel reads them. Backups and extracts are further copies a `DELETE` never reaches.

choices.text: `count(*)` still includes the rows, since it is answered from the row counts in the log
choices.why: The delete's commit removes the old files from the table and adds the new ones with their own counts, so the count drops at once.

choices.text: The rows are out of the files but still written in the log's `remove` actions
choices.why: A `remove` names a file by its path. It carries no rows.

prompt: The nightly scoring job appends to a Delta table with `txnAppId` set to `lapse-scores` and `txnVersion` to the night, `20260228`. A bug in the features is fixed, and the job is run again for 28 February with the same options. What does the table hold for that night?
hint: Big Data and Distributed Processing, lesson 11; Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 8.

choices.text: The first run's scores, untouched
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The corrected scores, in place of the first run's
choices.why: The pair marks a write as already done, not a night to replace. The second write is skipped, and replacing the night means deleting its rows first.

choices.text: Both runs' scores, so every member twice
choices.why: That is a plain append run twice; the pair in the log is exactly what stops it here.

choices.text: Nothing at all: a repeated `txnVersion` fails the write and rolls back the first one
choices.why: The second attempt is skipped without an error, and a commit already in the log is not undone by a later write.

prompt: A Structured Streaming query with a five-second `processingTime` trigger appends to a Delta table, and each batch's tasks write their own files. A month on, one day's query opens thousands of tiny files. Which fix leaves the stream as it is and gives readers large files?
hint: Big Data and Distributed Processing, lesson 11; Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 12.

choices.text: `coalesce(1)` on every batch, so each writes a single file
choices.why: One file every five seconds is still 17,280 files a day.

choices.text: A larger `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` for the readers
choices.why: Packing more files into a task still opens every file and reads every footer; the files stay as small as they were.

choices.text: Writing plain Parquet instead, whose `_spark_metadata` merges each batch's files
choices.why: `_spark_metadata` lists the files of each finished batch. It merges nothing.

choices.text: Running `OPTIMIZE` on a schedule of its own, apart from the writes
choices.why: Right.

prompt: On YARN, an application asks for executors of 512 MB and leaves the overhead at its default. What does each executor's container count against the queue?

choices.why: A container is the heap plus an overhead for thread stacks, network buffers and native libraries.

choices.text: About 896 MB: the heap, and at least 384 MB for what lies outside it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: About 563 MB: the heap, plus a tenth of the executor's memory on top
choices.why: The overhead is a tenth of the memory or 384 MB, whichever is larger, and a tenth of 512 is far below the floor.

choices.text: Less than 512 MB, because Spark reserves 300 MB of every heap for its own objects
choices.why: The reserve is carved out of the heap. YARN counts the whole heap, and the overhead beside it.

prompt: Stock is kept per shop, and the topic is keyed by shop. Recife sends five copies of a book to Olinda. How does lesson 2 put the transfer into the log?

choices.why: Right.

choices.text: As one event keyed by `recife`, the shop the books leave.

prompt: A customer asks to be erased. Their purchases are in the `sales` topic, which has `cleanup.policy=delete`, a `retention.ms` of seven days and the default `segment.ms` of seven days. Which sentence belongs in the answer the customer receives?
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 3; Data Security, Governance and Privacy, lesson 7.

choices.text: They have been deleted: a delete was written for each of the customer's sales.
choices.why: Kafka has no way to delete one message, and a message with a key and no value only means something on a compacted topic.

choices.text: They are gone, because every consumer group has already read them.
choices.why: Reading never removed anything; retention does not care who has read what.

choices.text: They stay in the topic until their segment expires, up to two weeks after each sale, and then they are gone.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They will be gone within minutes, once `retention.ms` on the topic is lowered to one hour and the broker checks again.
choices.why: Retention removes whole segments, every customer's sales with them, and keeps the last hour; that empties the topic, not the customer's data.

prompt: A consumer of a three-partition topic keyed by shop is too slow, so a teammate has its one member hand each message to whichever of eight threads is free. The stock it keeps per shop starts to come out wrong. Why, by lesson 4?

choices.text: The group rebalances whenever a thread picks up a message, and the partitions stop while it does.
choices.why: A rebalance follows members joining or leaving; threads inside one member are not members.

choices.text: The member now receives each partition's messages out of offset order.
choices.why: The member still receives them in offset order; the order is lost afterwards, between the threads.

choices.text: Two sales of one shop go to two threads at once and finish in either order.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The sale is accepted, with one copy on one disk.

prompt: A partition's leader is killed while a producer with `acks=all` is sending to it. Put what follows in order, by lesson 5.

A new leader is picked from the partition's ISR
Every node is told who the new leader is

choices.text: It accepts version 2 as a minor change, the way a contract treats a new optional field.

choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It accepts it, and readers still on version 1 fail to decode the new sales.

prompt: Five-minute tumbling windows, a watermark bound of two minutes, and five minutes of allowed lateness. A sale for the 09:05 to 09:10 window arrives late. It can still update that window until the latest event time seen reaches what time? Give it in minutes after 09:00.
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 11.

prompt: A Structured Streaming query appends its counts as files to a directory, and another engine reads that directory by listing every file in it. A crash interrupts a batch halfway through. What can that engine end up counting, and what avoids it?
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 12; Big Data and Distributed Processing, lesson 11.

choices.text: The files of the interrupted batch, which no `_spark_metadata` entry names; a reader that goes by a log of commits leaves them out.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing extra: the file sink is exactly-once, so every reader sees each window once.
choices.why: It is exactly-once for a reader that goes by `_spark_metadata`; a plain listing takes every file it finds.

choices.text: Windows still open, which the next batch rewrites once the watermark has passed them.
choices.why: In append mode a window is written once, after the watermark passes it, and a file is never rewritten.

choices.text: Each window twice, unless the query switches to update mode and overwrites its files.
choices.why: A file cannot be updated, and the file sink refuses update mode before the query starts.

prompt: A Kafka Streams application counts sales per book, reading a topic keyed by shop. `groupBy` picks the book as the new key, so the library writes every sale to Kafka a second time, keyed by book. Lesson 13 calls that topic the ___ topic.
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 13.

prompt: A Debezium connector reads only the `stock` table, which changes once a day. Connect is running and the slot shows `active` as `t`, yet its retained WAL grows all night while another application writes gigabytes to tables nobody publishes. Why, and what does lesson 14 set?
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 14.

choices.text: The slot moves only when the connector confirms a change from its own tables; `heartbeat.interval.ms` makes it confirm on a timer.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The other application's tables were added to the publication by mistake, and removing them stops it.
choices.why: Unpublished tables' WAL is held all the same: the WAL is one stream for the whole server.

choices.text: `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` on `stock` writes old rows into the WAL; going back to `DEFAULT` frees it.
choices.why: FULL adds the old row to that table's updates and deletes, once a day here; it holds nothing back.

choices.text: The connector has fallen behind, and `max_slot_wal_keep_size` lets it catch up.
choices.why: There is nothing waiting to be read; and that setting saves the disk by marking the slot lost.

prompt: Packing an order takes 40 seconds, and the SQS queue's visibility timeout is 30. Nothing crashes. What happens, by lesson 15?
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 15.

choices.text: Nothing: a packer still at work keeps the order hidden until it deletes it.
choices.why: SQS has no connection to watch; it uses the clock, and after 30 seconds the order is visible again.

choices.text: Every order is lost, because SQS deletes a message whose timeout runs out.
choices.why: A message whose timeout runs out becomes visible again; it is only deleted by a consumer.

choices.text: Every order is handed to a second packer while the first is still on it.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The second packer is refused the order, since the first has acknowledged it.
choices.why: SQS has no acknowledgement; a consumer deletes the message when the work is done.

prompt: The website promises that its stock is never more than a minute old. A teammate proposes paging on-call whenever the `stock` group's lag passes 1000 messages. What do the two lessons page on instead?
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 16; Observability and Operations, lesson 16.

choices.text: Lag in time above a few minutes: the stale stock a customer sees, whatever caused it.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A higher count, say 10 000, so that Saturday morning's peak, which drains on its own, wakes nobody.
choices.why: A count says nothing about staleness: a thousand messages is a second on a busy topic and hours on a quiet one.

choices.text: Each cause separately, each with its own threshold: a rebalance, a slow database, a poison message.
choices.why: Causes are tickets; one page on the symptom covers every cause, including the ones nobody listed.

choices.text: The consumer's rate, against the rate it managed at launch.
choices.why: A rate belongs on a dashboard; it does not say whether the promise to the customer is broken.

prompt: Sales cross Kafka with a `traceparent` header. Lesson 16's counter copies a bad sale to `sales.dlq` with its key, its value and two headers of its own, the error and where the sale came from. Once the sale is fixed and sent back, what does its trace look like?
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 16; Observability and Operations, lesson 4.

choices.text: The original trace, with a gap for the time the sale sat in the dead-letter topic.
choices.why: Only a context carried inside the message joins a trace, and the copy's headers were replaced, not added to.

choices.text: A new trace: the copy carried no `traceparent`.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The original trace, found through the `from` header's partition and offset.
choices.why: An origin is not a trace context; nothing extracts a trace from it.

choices.text: No trace at all, because a consumer cannot open a span for a message without one.
choices.why: Extracting from missing headers gives an empty context, and the span starts a trace of its own.

prompt: A new version of the stock program reprocesses `sales` from the start under the group `stock-v2` while the old one keeps serving. Taking blue-green as the deployment lesson runs it, the team lets both versions write to the one `stock` table they share. What goes wrong?
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 16; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 10.

choices.text: The table mixes both versions' numbers while the new one catches up, and no row says which wrote it.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing, since the new group has offsets of its own and leaves the old group alone.
choices.why: Separate offsets keep the reading apart, not the writing; two versions writing to one place leave a mixture of both.

choices.text: Nothing, provided the new version is idempotent, since a repeat then changes nothing.
choices.why: Idempotence stops repeats; here two different programs write different numbers to the same rows.

choices.text: The old group is moved back to the start as well, and the stock page shows Monday's numbers until it catches up.
choices.why: A new group changes nothing about the old one; moving a group back is replay.

prompt: Ponto Final keeps its 20 000 sales a day for seven days, in three copies. Lesson 17 measured about 135 bytes a sale on disk uncompressed, and 17 with `zstd` after rounding. How many megabytes of disk does `zstd` save, all copies counted? (1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes)
hint: Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 17.

prompt: `python -m pytest -q --durations=4` on `shipquote` lists two teardowns of 0.50 s each at the top, while the acceptance test's six quotes take 0.03 s together. What does that say about the top of the pyramid?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 1.

choices.text: The requests are what is slow, and a quicker HTTP server would fix it.
choices.why: The six requests cost 0.03 s together; the half seconds belong to shutting the server down.

choices.text: Teardown time is noise pytest adds to every test; only the `call` entries are worth reading.
choices.why: The teardowns are the real cost: `serve_forever` checks every half second whether it should stop, once per module.

choices.text: The integration layer's SQLite is the bottleneck of the whole suite.
choices.why: The three integration tests took 0.17 s; SQLite lives in the test's own process and costs almost nothing.

choices.text: Its cost is in setting up and tearing down a world for the tests, and it multiplies with every module up there.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A Spark job sends each customer a confirmation e-mail from inside a task. Its unit test hands the task a spy for the mailer, asserts exactly one call per order, and passes. In the cluster, some customers get two e-mails on the night an executor is killed. Why could the test not see it?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 2; Big Data and Distributed Processing, lesson 2.

choices.text: A spy only records calls; a mock built with `create_autospec` would have checked them and failed.
choices.why: The test did read the spy's record and asserted one call. The problem is not who checks, it is that the cluster ran the code twice.

choices.text: The spy replaced the mailer, so the test never met the real SMTP server, which resends a message it did not hear back about.
choices.why: Nothing in the story points at the mail server. A task that sends as a side effect sends again when Spark retries it.

choices.text: Spark restarts the whole job when an executor dies, so every order was processed twice.
choices.why: Only the tasks running on that executor are lost and rerun; finished tasks had already sent their results. That is why only some customers got two.

choices.text: Spark reran the lost task from its input, so the e-mail inside it went out again; the test ran each task once.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: For a staging database, a team copies production's orders and replaces `customer_id` with `md5(customer_id::text)`, so the orders still join to each other. The customer ids run from 1 to 6,012. What is wrong with this test data?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 3; Data Security, Governance and Privacy, lesson 5.

choices.text: Nothing: once hashed, the copy is anonymous and the LGPD no longer reaches it.
choices.why: An unkeyed hash of a small, known range is the value written differently. And even a proper pseudonym is still personal data.

choices.text: Keeping the joins is the mistake; a fixture should not relate one table to another.
choices.why: Relationships surviving is what anonymising consistently is for. The flaw is that the people survive too.

choices.text: `md5` is too slow for a table this size; an HMAC would make the copy anonymous and safe to commit as a fixture.
choices.why: A keyed HMAC is a real pseudonym, and pseudonymised data is still personal data: it does not belong in a repository.

choices.text: Hashing 1 to 6,012 returns every customer in a second; test data should be generated, not copied.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A pull request adds a surcharge for parcels over 30 kg to `freight`: an `if` and the `return` under it, with no new test. The total goes from 81% to 80%, and `coverage report -m` names only the `return` as missing. What should the reviewer conclude?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 4.

choices.text: Half the change is tested, since the `if` is covered.
choices.why: The `if` ran because every quote passes through it, and no quote went over 30 kg. A line that ran is not a line that was checked.

choices.text: None of the new behaviour was tested; nobody has checked what a heavy parcel costs.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing about this change: a one-point drop in the total is what any change on a large project looks like.
choices.why: That is why the total is the wrong thing to read. The changed file's missing lines speak about this change.

choices.text: The `return` deserves `# pragma: no cover`, because parcels that heavy are rare and the line would only add noise to the report.
choices.why: An exclusion is for code not worth testing. A price is worth testing, and hiding the line hides the gap.

prompt: Which of these earn an exclusion from the coverage count? Choose all that apply.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 4.

choices.text: An `assert False` marking a branch that cannot happen.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `main()`, which reads `SHIPQUOTE_PORT` and builds the server.
choices.why: Both can be wrong, a typo in the variable or a server on the wrong address. Excluding it hides it from the one report that shows nothing checks it yet.

choices.text: Code under `if TYPE_CHECKING:`, read by type checkers only.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The handling of a carrier error that no test has reached yet.
choices.why: Untested is not the same as not worth testing. That missing line is a test to write.

choices.text: The `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard at the foot of `app.py`.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: This repository's CI runs on `pull_request` to `main` and again on `push` to `main`. Why check the code a second time, after it merges?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5.

choices.text: The pull request run uses a cached checkout, and only the push run starts from what was committed.
choices.why: Every run starts from a clean checkout. A cache holds dependencies, never the code under test.

choices.text: A push to `main` is what builds and publishes the release.
choices.why: A release is started by a tag starting with `v`, which then calls the same checks.

choices.text: Each change passed alone; combined, the two are code nobody has tested yet.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A pull request run cannot be a required check.
choices.why: Required checks are exactly the ones a pull request must pass before it merges.

prompt: Every matrix cell uploads its `.coverage.*` file as an artifact, and a coverage job downloads them all and runs `coverage combine`. The upload step has no `include-hidden-files: true`. What happens?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 6.

choices.text: The upload fails, naming the hidden files it skipped, and the whole run goes red at that step.
choices.why: Nothing fails. The upload action leaves hidden files out quietly unless told otherwise.

choices.text: The coverage job reads the files from the cells' machines instead, since they ran in the same workflow.
choices.why: Jobs do not share files: each machine is discarded at the end, and artifacts are the only way across.

choices.text: `merge-multiple` keeps one file of the six, so only one cell is counted.
choices.why: `merge-multiple` puts the artifacts' files into one directory; the files here never reached an artifact at all.

choices.text: The dot-files are left out, so `coverage combine` has nothing and every job stays green.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Put the stages of a delivery pipeline in the order every team keeps, whatever else differs.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7.
items: Build the artifact from the commit, once
Test it, in the matrix
Deploy it to staging and smoke-test it there
Pass the gate
Deploy the same artifact to production and smoke-test it
trap: Testing before building reads naturally, but what is tested has to be the bytes that ship; and the gate comes after staging because it decides on an artifact already proved deployable.

prompt: A team applies lesson 7's expand then contract to an Avro event rather than a table, replacing the field `cents` with `amount`: producers write both for a while, consumers move to `amount`, and `cents` is dropped last. Which step of the table version has no counterpart on the topic?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7; Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 6.

choices.text: The expand, because the registry refuses any new field under `BACKWARD`.
choices.why: A new field with a default passes `BACKWARD`; it is a field with no default that the registry refuses.

choices.text: The contract, since a field can never leave a subject once registered.
choices.why: Removing a field is allowed under `BACKWARD`, and a field that had a default may go under `FORWARD`.

choices.text: The backfill: a topic is not migrated, and messages written before `amount` existed keep their schema for as long as retention keeps them.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: None of them: accepting a version rewrites the stored messages in it.
choices.why: The registry checks schemas when a version is offered; the bytes on the topic stay as they were written.

prompt: Your service's `/health` returns `{"status": "ok"}` whenever the process answers HTTP, like the storefront's in observability lesson 14. After a deploy its database is unreachable and every request on the main path fails, yet a smoke test shaped like `ops/smoke.sh` passes. What does the smoke test lack?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7; Observability and Operations, lesson 14.

choices.text: A longer `--max-time`, so the health check waits for the database to come up.
choices.why: The check answered at once and said `ok`. Waiting longer for the same question gets the same answer.

choices.text: One real read through the route customers depend on, such as a quote for a known CEP.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing: a smoke test only asks whether the program is up, and the database is the integration tests' business.
choices.why: Integration tests never meet the deployed configuration. The smoke test is the one check that runs against it.

choices.text: A comparison of `/version` against the artifact's SHA-256 rather than its version number.
choices.why: The version was right; the release was the one meant. What nobody asked was whether it can do its job.

prompt: A staging service was deployed with production's database address and password, copied from the wrong file, and wrote test orders into production. Which control would have stopped it?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 8; Data Security, Governance and Privacy, lesson 1.

choices.text: Revoking `CONNECT` on production's database from `PUBLIC`, so that no role connects unless named.
choices.why: The service logged in as the application's own role, which is granted `CONNECT` by name. Turning the default around does not stop a named role.

choices.text: A smoke test in staging that checks `/version` right after each deploy finishes.
choices.why: The version was the one meant, so the check passes. A smoke test asks whether the program answers, not where its data lives.

choices.text: Masking the customers in staging's own copy, so nothing personal sits there.
choices.why: Masking protects the copy staging holds. Here staging was writing to production, and no copy was involved.

choices.text: Production's `pg_hba.conf` admitting the app only from production.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: For a leaked pipeline token, lesson 9 says revoke or rotate first, accepting a short outage. The same week an OpenBao transit key is suspected exposed, and somebody follows that order: rotate it, then set `min_decryption_version=2` at once, planning to rewrap later. What does that cost here?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9; Data Security, Governance and Privacy, lesson 4.

choices.text: A short outage, until every service has the new key version in its configuration.
choices.why: Services never hold the key, and new encryptions already use version 2. The damage is to what was encrypted before.

choices.text: Nothing, since old ciphertext keeps decrypting after a rotation.
choices.why: That is true of a rotation alone. Raising the minimum is what stops version 1 from decrypting.

choices.text: Every `v1` ciphertext is refused as too old: data lost, not paused.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The rewrap, done afterwards, shows the plaintext to the operator who runs it.
choices.why: A rewrap keeps the plaintext inside OpenBao for the length of the call, and after the minimum is raised it cannot read `v1` at all.

prompt: A pipeline deploys a website that encrypts CPFs through OpenBao. Which of these follow least privilege? Choose all that apply.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9; Data Security, Governance and Privacy, lesson 4.

choices.text: `permissions: contents: read` at the top of the workflow, with `id-token: write` added in the deploy job alone.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `contents: write` at the top of the workflow, so the one job that creates the release has it.
choices.why: A permission set for the workflow reaches every job, including a test job running a compromised dependency. It belongs on the job that needs it.

choices.text: A policy giving the website `update` on `transit/encrypt/ipe-cpf` and nothing on `transit/decrypt/ipe-cpf`.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A token for the website that may also read `transit/keys/ipe-cpf`, to check the key's version before it encrypts.
choices.why: Using a key does not need its configuration; the ciphertext already says which version made it.

prompt: `ops/canary.py` refuses to judge a side that has answered fewer than 50 requests. A service takes ten requests a minute, and its canary gets 1% of them. How many minutes pass before the canary can be judged?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 10.

prompt: A team ships version 2 of a lapse model behind a web service with a canary rule like `ops/canary.py`: stop when the canary's error rate is more than a point above the baseline's. Version 2 answers every request with a 200, and gives most of its members a probability over 0.2. What does the rule see?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 10; Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 8.

choices.text: Nothing; what each side says has to be set side by side instead, such as the average per group.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A breach: probabilities that high are counted as errors.
choices.why: An error here is a 5xx or no answer. A 200 carrying a strange number passes every error count.

choices.text: Nothing yet: it should wait about 90 days for the labels, then compare which version was right.
choices.why: Nobody has to wait for labels. A version whose outputs look nothing like the stable one's is stopped on what it says.

choices.text: Nothing, because it splits per request; splitting by member would make the error rate show the bug.
choices.why: Splitting by member keeps each person on one side. It changes who sees which version, not what an error count can measure.

prompt: A flag that turns off something expensive or fragile under pressure, such as the carrier call, and may stay in the code for years, is an operational flag, also called a kill ___.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 10.

prompt: A column has to go from `cents` to `price_cents`, and a rollback must stay safe at every step. Put the releases in order.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11.
items: Add `price_cents` beside `cents`
Write both columns, still reading `cents`
Copy the old rows' values into `price_cents`
Read `price_cents`
Stop writing `cents`, and drop it in a later release
trap: Copying the old rows before the code writes both leaves a gap: whatever is written in between has no `price_cents`. And the drop is last because it is the one step the release before cannot survive.

prompt: A release goes to a canary on 5% of checkouts and fails one request in twenty there; the other 95% are fine. The checkout objective is 99.5%. What burn rate does that produce, and what should stop the release?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11; Observability and Operations, lesson 16.

choices.text: About 10, high enough to page the on-call, who then stops the release.
choices.why: One in twenty is the canary's rate. Over all checkouts it is 5% of 5%, 0.25%, against an allowed 0.5%.

choices.text: About 0.5, so it is safe to promote, since the month's budget is not at risk.
choices.why: The budget is safe at 5%. At 100% the same release fails 5% of checkouts, a burn rate of 10.

choices.text: About 0.5, too low to page; the canary's comparison with the baseline must stop it.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: None can be computed yet: the canary has to answer 50 requests before any rate means something.
choices.why: Fifty is the canary's own evidence rule. A burn rate is undefined only with no traffic at all.

prompt: `ops/canary.py` stops when the canary's error rate is more than `MAX_GAP = 1.0` point above the baseline's. For a single error never to cross that gap on its own, `MIN_REQUESTS` has to be at least ___ answers.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11.

prompt: Match each piece of the model pipeline to the release idea from this course that it plays.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7; Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 7.

pairs.left: `models:/lapse@champion`, a name `set_registered_model_alias` can point at any version
pairs.right: A tag such as `shipquote:1.4.0`, which anybody with write access can move

pairs.left: The MD5 that `dvc.lock` records for `models/lapse.joblib`
pairs.right: The SHA-256 written beside the tarball, naming those exact bytes

pairs.left: `log_run.py` refusing to run while `git status --porcelain` prints anything
pairs.right: `git archive` writing what is committed and nothing else

right_distractors: A smoke test asking `/version` after the deploy

prompt: Lesson 1 moves from one signal to the next through what each pair has in common. Match each pair of signals to what joins it.
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 1.

pairs.left: A trace and a log line
pairs.right: the trace id written in every line

pairs.left: A metric and a trace
pairs.right: the service and a time window

pairs.left: A metric and a log line
pairs.right: the service name, and almost nothing else

right_distractors: the span id of the request's first span

prompt: The Collector stops answering for ten minutes while payments keeps taking charges, exporting through the batch span processor. What does payments' SDK do with the spans it finishes in that time?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 2.

choices.text: It keeps a fixed number in its queue, 2048 by default in Python, and drops the rest.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Each request waits for its export to go through, so charges slow down until the Collector is back.
choices.why: Waiting on the network is the simple processor's habit; the batch one queues the span and returns at once.

choices.text: It grows the queue as far as it needs and sends everything when the Collector returns.
choices.why: The queue is bounded on purpose: a service that ran out of memory because its telemetry could not be delivered is the wrong failure.

choices.text: It writes them to disk and sends them after the next restart.
choices.why: Nothing in the SDK keeps the queue on disk; a process that dies loses whatever was still waiting in it.

prompt: A new panel filters spans on `http.request.method`. It shows the storefront's requests and none of orders', although both services are traced. Why, by lesson 3?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 3.

choices.text: Flask's instrumentation records no method at all; only spans written by hand carry one.
choices.why: Orders' `POST /orders` span does carry the method; lesson 3 listed its keys, `http.method` among them.

choices.text: The automatic instrumentation there still writes the older name, `http.method`.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Orders excludes its routes from tracing with `OTEL_PYTHON_FLASK_EXCLUDED_URLS`.
choices.why: That variable leaves out `health` and `metrics` only; the order route is traced.

choices.text: The conventions name the method one way on a server span and another way on a client span.
choices.why: The difference is a generation of names, not a kind of span: orders' server and client spans both use the older one.

prompt: A team moves the order confirmations from RabbitMQ to a Kafka topic and wants the mailer's spans to stay in the checkout's trace. Kafka records carry headers, as the streaming course's dead-letter topic showed. Where does the context travel, and what does the consumer do with it?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 4; Streaming and Event Processing, lesson 16.

choices.text: Nowhere extra: the group's committed offset already ties each record to the request that wrote it.
choices.why: An offset is a position in a partition; it knows nothing about the trace of whoever produced the record.

choices.text: In the record's headers: the producer injects it, and the receiving side extracts it and starts its span under it.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It is read from the record's timestamp, which the producer sets from the trace.
choices.why: The timestamp says when the record was created; the trace id is 128 random bits that only a `traceparent` carries.

choices.text: The consumer extracts it from `TRACEPARENT` and `TRACESTATE` in its own environment, as a child process would.
choices.why: That convention passes the context to a child process started by a traced parent; a message has to carry its own.

prompt: The morning Spark report runs on a cluster created for the job and deleted when it ends, as the big data course describes. How can Prometheus say that the report did not run last night?
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 5; Big Data and Distributed Processing, lesson 14.

choices.text: Scrape the driver while it runs: `up` falling to 0 afterwards shows that it ran.
choices.why: Once the cluster is deleted the target is gone whether or not the report finished; `up` cannot tell a job that ended from one that never started.

choices.text: A last-success timestamp pushed to the Pushgateway, and an alert on the time since it.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Trace each run, with links to what it read, and alert when a night has no trace.
choices.why: A trace exists only for work that happened; nothing in a trace store notices one that is missing.

choices.text: The job pushes a counter of its runs to the Pushgateway, and an alert compares it with the day before.
choices.why: Each run is a new process, so the counter it pushes reads 1 every night; a timestamp grows every second whatever happens.

prompt: Because Prometheus asks each target for its numbers, it knows when one stops answering, and on every scrape it records that as a metric of its own named ___, 1 or 0 for each target.
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 5.

prompt: The lapse service of the machine learning course logs `path`, `status`, `ms`, `p_lapse` and `model_version` for every request. A team turns fields like these into labels on a Prometheus request counter. Which labels are safe to keep? Choose all that apply.
hint: Observability and Operations, lesson 6; Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 9.

choices.text: `member_id`, to count one member's requests
choices.why: Lesson 6's `user_id` experiment: a label per person is a series per person, and anything that names one member goes on the span or the line.

choices.text: `path`, as the log writes it

hint: Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 8; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11.

choices.text: It is promoted: every answer is a 200, and the criteria count only errors.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It is stopped at 25%, as the shipping release that could not quote Alagoas was.
choices.why: That release failed requests. Version 2 fails none, so the error rule never fires.

choices.text: It is stopped at 5%, the first step, where the canary has too few answers to judge.
choices.why: Too few answers makes the script carry on to the next step, not stop.

choices.text: It cannot run: a model service has no error rate to compare.
choices.why: It has one, from the status of every request. Errors are just not what is wrong with version 2.

prompt: Support wants each member's lapse probability beside their tickets in the help desk. One proposal calls lesson 8's web service for every ticket; another copies a field into the help desk. Which design do the two courses point to?
hint: Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 8; Analytics, BI and Reverse ETL, lesson 7.

choices.text: The web service, because a probability shown to support has to be computed when the ticket opens.
choices.why: The score can be no fresher than its features, which change nightly, and a service adds an outage the table never had.

choices.text: A nightly sync of `lapse_scores`, keyed by member id, sending only the rows that changed.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A sync keyed by the member's e-mail address, which support already searches by.
choices.why: People change and share addresses. The shop's own id is assigned once and never changes.

choices.text: A sync that sends every member's row on every run, so that the help desk is never out of date.
choices.why: Resending everything is slower, spends requests the API limits, and overwrites whatever somebody typed in those fields.

prompt: The lapse service's objective is lesson 9's: 99.9% of requests not answered with a 5xx. In one hour it answers 20,000 requests: 13,000 with a 200, 6,960 with a 404 for members the online store has nothing fresh for, and 40 with a 500. What is that hour's burn rate?
hint: Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 9; Observability and Operations, lesson 16.

prompt: With sixteen requests in flight, the lapse service's p99 is 351.8 ms, against 10.8 ms one at a time. Which change shortens that wait, and what does it cost?
hint: Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 9.

choices.text: More threads inside the one process, which costs nothing extra in memory.
choices.why: Python runs one thread of Python code at a time, so the predictions still take turns, and switching costs something too.

choices.text: Loading the model once at start-up rather than on every request.
choices.why: `serve.py` already does that. The wait is queueing behind other predictions.

choices.text: Raising the objective to 400 ms, so that the number passes.
choices.why: That moves the promise and leaves the wait where it was.

choices.text: More worker processes, each with its own model, paid for in memory.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: The watch passed every night from March to June. A colleague proposes shortening its reference from the 28 days before each night to the 7 days before. What would that do to the slow rise in `online_share`?
hint: Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 10.

choices.text: Catch it sooner, because a shorter window reacts faster to whatever changes.
choices.why: Reacting faster catches a sudden break. A slow change is a few per cent a week whatever the window.

choices.text: Hide it even better, since last week's members have moved almost as far as tonight's.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Catch it from mid-March, the week postage on online orders became free.
choices.why: Each week then moved only a little from the one before, which a moving reference cannot see.

choices.text: Nothing, because the watch compares the scores and not the inputs.
choices.why: It compares the median of every numeric input too. The trouble is what it compares them with.

prompt: Which of these changes could be found only in the outcomes, ninety days late, and not in the inputs? Choose all that apply.
hint: Machine Learning and MLOps, lesson 10.

choices.text: A load multiplies every `spend_180d` by a hundred.

choices.text: Free postage moves members from the shops to the website.

choices.text: A rival's book subscription draws away young members whose histories look as they always did.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A new channel, `app`, appears among the members.
choices.why: A value the training data never had is an input; `channel` measured 0.420 on the first night.

choices.text: A price rise makes members with the same visits and spend come back less often than before.
choices.why: Right.
